grayston.brief_markdown:
# Case Brief of R v Grayston

## Preliminary Information
- **Name and Citation of Case:** *R v Grayston*, 2016 ONCA 784
- **Date of Decision:** October 26, 2016
- **Parties:**
  - Her Majesty the Queen – respondent
  - Frank Joseph Grayston – appellant

## Legal Issue(s)
- Whether the verdict is unreasonable or cannot be supported by the evidence within the meaning of s. 686(1)(a)(i) of the Criminal Code. (¶2)
  - Specifically, whether the inference that the appellant was wearing or had the balaclava with him in connection with the theft of the Sunbird is a more likely inference than the inference that he was in contact with the balaclava on an unrelated occasion. (¶16)
  - Specifically, whether the appellant's guilt was the only rational conclusion available on the totality of the evidence. (¶16)

## Facts of the case
- Between midnight and 5:00 a.m. on February 18, 2015, a 1988 Pontiac Sunbird was taken from the premises of the Barton Truck company; around the same time and in the same vicinity, an attempted break and enter of a jewellery store and a robbery of a large quantity of drugs from a pharmacy took place. (¶4)
- On February 20, 2015 the Sunbird was located abandoned in a parking lot, police found a black skeletal balaclava in the car, and investigation led the police to the appellant's apartment where they discovered drugs. (¶5)
- DNA from inside the balaclava around the mouth area showed a mixture of DNA from at least three individuals; the one profile determined for comparison matched the appellant's DNA to a degree of statistical certainty. (¶6)
- The appellant was charged with various offences arising out of the theft of the Sunbird, the robbery of the pharmacy and the attempted break and enter of the jewellery store. (¶7)
- To establish that the appellant participated in the theft of the Sunbird, the prosecution relied on the DNA evidence and the fact that the attempted break and enter of the jewellery store and the robbery of the pharmacy took place close to where the car was stolen; the appellant neither testified nor called any evidence. (¶8)

## Ratio Decidendi
- The Crown must demonstrate first that, based on the evidence, the inference that the accused was in contact with the object bearing his DNA in connection with the offence is a more likely inference than the inference that he was in contact with it on an unrelated occasion, and second that the accused's guilt is the only rational conclusion available on the totality of the evidence. (¶16)
- The Crown cannot point to any evidence that makes the inference that the appellant was in contact with the garment in connection with the theft more likely than the inference that he was in contact with the balaclava at some other time; evidence of his DNA on the balaclava only demonstrates that he likely wore the garment at some point in time, and the discovery of the balaclava in the abandoned stolen car, by itself, did not permit any such inference. (¶17)
- The proximity between the Barton Truck company premises, where the Sunbird was stolen, and the jewellery store and pharmacy is of no relevance given the trial judge was not satisfied that the evidence supported a finding that the appellant was at all connected with the other thefts. (¶19)
- While the evidence supported the inference that the appellant had worn the balaclava at some point, there was insufficient evidence to support an inference that he was wearing it or otherwise was in possession of it at the time the car was stolen. (¶20)

## Decision
- There was an insufficient evidentiary footing for the trial judge to conclude that the appellant's guilt was the only reasonable conclusion available on the totality of the evidence, and his conviction is therefore unreasonable within the meaning of s. 686(1)(a)(i). (¶20)

kazemi.brief_markdown:
# Case Brief of R v Kazemi

## Preliminary Information
- **Name and Citation of Case:** *R v Kazemi*, 2013 ONCA 585
- **Date of Decision:** September 27, 2013
- **Parties:**
  - Her Majesty the Queen – appellant
  - Khojasteh Kazemi – respondent

## Legal Issue(s)
- Whether the respondent was "holding" a hand-held wireless communication device for the purposes of s. 78.1(1) of the Highway Traffic Act. (¶3)
  - Specifically, whether "holding" requires some sustained physical holding of the device, as the appeal judge held, or is satisfied by having the device in one's hand at all while driving. (¶15)

## Facts of the case
- On April 26, 2010, the respondent was driving home from work alone and, while stopped at a stop light, a police officer observed her to have a cell phone in her hand; she said the phone had been on the seat, dropped to the floor when she braked, and she picked it up at the red light. (¶1)
- The respondent was charged with driving while holding a hand-held wireless communication device pursuant to s. 78.1(1) of the Highway Traffic Act. (¶2)
- The respondent does not contest that when she was observed by the officer she was driving, and that her cell phone was a hand-held wireless communication device. (¶3)

## Ratio Decidendi
- The ordinary meaning of "holding" a cell phone is having it in one's hand; there is no suggestion that only if one has the cell phone in one's hand for a sustained period of time is one holding the cell phone. (¶11)
- This interpretation of "holding" best ensures the attainment of the objective of the HTA, which is to protect those who use the roads of Ontario. (¶12)
- This interpretation also best serves the legislature's purpose in enacting the provision in which "holding" appears, being eyes-on-the-road, hands-on-the-wheel legislation aimed at stopping the use of hand-held wireless communication devices while driving. (¶13)
- Road safety is best ensured by a complete prohibition on having a cell phone in one's hand at all while driving, which eliminates any risk of distraction by the information on the cell phone, removes any temptation to use it, and prevents any possibility of it physically interfering with the driver's ability to drive. (¶14)
- An interpretation requiring sustained physical holding would exempt any holding for a shorter period of time, with the accompanying risks to road safety and driver attention, and does not accord with the ordinary meaning of the word or properly reflect the object of the HTA. (¶15)

## Decision
- The appeal judge erred in his interpretation of "holding" in s. 78.1(1) of the HTA; the correct interpretation is that holding a cell phone means having it in one's hand, with no requirement of a sustained period. (¶16)
